phil-ea-01-c1.text: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Confucius. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
phil-ea-01-c1.quote: Do not impose upon others those things that you yourself do not desire
phil-ea-01-c1.claim: 'Do not do to others what you do not wish for yourself' is Confucius's negative formulation of the Golden Rule.

phil-ea-01-c2.text: Jeff Richey. Confucius (551–479 B.C.E.). Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
phil-ea-01-c2.quote: Let the ruler be a ruler, the subject a subject, a father a father, and a son a son.
phil-ea-01-c2.claim: when a father is truly a father and a ruler truly a ruler.

phil-ea-01-c3.text: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Mencius. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
phil-ea-01-c3.claim: Mencius (Mèngzǐ, 4th c. BCE) argued that human nature is originally good.

phil-ea-01-c3.text: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Mencius. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
phil-ea-01-c3.quote: The feeling of compassion is benevolence.
phil-ea-01-c3.claim: His famous example is a child about to fall into a well.

phil-ea-01-c3.text: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Xunzi. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
phil-ea-01-c3.quote: Human xing is evil; what is good is artifice.
phil-ea-01-c3.claim: Human nature is bad, he said, because we're born with appetites that, left unchecked, produce conflict.

phil-ea-03-c2.text: Dalal, Neil (2021). Śaṅkara. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
phil-ea-03-c2.quote: In Śaṅkara’s final philosophical position, there is only brahman without parts, attributes, or causation.
phil-ea-03-c2.claim: For Śaṅkara only Brahman is truly real.

phil-ea-04-c3.text: Westerhoff, Jan Christoph (2010). Nāgārjuna. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
phil-ea-04-c3.quote: the questions Nāgārjuna asked and the system of philosophy he founded in the second century remain very much alive in the twenty-first
phil-ea-04-c3.claim: Nāgārjuna (ca. 2nd–3rd c. CE) founded the Madhyamaka school of Mahāyāna Buddhism.
